claim: 433 acute serum samples from 595 virologically-confirmed dengue (VCD) cases in CYD14 were selected for investigation.
source: 433 acute serum samples from 595 virologically-confirmed dengue (VCD) cases in CYD14 and 512 samples from 662 VCD cases in CYD15 were selected for investigation on the basis of subject consent, viremia level and sample volume considerations (Figure 1A and B, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples and cases from CYD14 trial.

claim: 512 acute serum samples from 662 VCD cases in CYD15 were selected for investigation.
source: 433 acute serum samples from 595 virologically-confirmed dengue (VCD) cases in CYD14 and 512 samples from 662 VCD cases in CYD15 were selected for investigation on the basis of subject consent, viremia level and sample volume considerations (Figure 1A and B, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples and cases from CYD15 trial.

claim: From CYD14, 314 complete DENV envelope (E) gene nucleotide sequences were acquired directly from 433 serum samples (72.5%).
source: From CYD14, 314 complete DENV envelope (E) gene nucleotide sequences (1485 nt for DENV-1,–2, −4; 1479 nt for DENV-3) were acquired directly from 433 serum samples (72.5%, including three mixed infections), with a subset of 299/433 (69.1%) samples also having a complete premembrane (prM) nucleotide sequence.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages of sequences obtained from CYD14 samples.

claim: Three mixed DENV infections were detected in CYD14 samples.
source: From CYD14, 314 complete DENV envelope (E) gene nucleotide sequences (1485 nt for DENV-1,–2, −4; 1479 nt for DENV-3) were acquired directly from 433 serum samples (72.5%, including three mixed infections), with a subset of 299/433 (69.1%) samples also having a complete premembrane (prM) nucleotide sequence.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of mixed infections detected.

claim: From CYD15, 333 complete DENV E gene nucleotide sequences were acquired directly from 512 serum samples (65.0%).
source: From CYD15, 333 complete DENV E gene nucleotide sequences were acquired directly from 512 serum samples (65.0%, including eight mixed infections), with a subset of 313/512 (61.1%) samples also having a complete prM nucleotide sequence.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages of sequences obtained from CYD15 samples.

claim: Eight mixed DENV infections were detected in CYD15 samples.
source: From CYD15, 333 complete DENV E gene nucleotide sequences were acquired directly from 512 serum samples (65.0%, including eight mixed infections), with a subset of 313/512 (61.1%) samples also having a complete prM nucleotide sequence.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of mixed infections detected.

claim: The proportion of serum samples that yielded an E gene sequence was similar between control and dengue vaccine recipients within each study.
source: The proportion of serum samples that yielded an E gene sequence was similar between control and dengue vaccine recipients within each study (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary data.

claim: The probability of acquiring an E gene sequence from serum samples was positively associated with the DENV viremia level.
source: The probability of acquiring an E gene sequence from serum samples was positively associated with the DENV viremia level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this association and references a figure showing the relationship.

claim: CYD14/15 viruses were closely related to publicly available DENV sequences acquired from the same country.
source: At the country level, CYD14/15 viruses were closely related to publicly available DENV sequences acquired from the same country, an indicator of ongoing local evolution.
evidence: The manuscript states this phylogenetic relationship based on sequence analysis.

claim: The mean level of E gene amino acid sequence difference between vaccine strains and viruses from VCD cases in CYD14 and CYD15 was <3% for all serotypes.
source: The mean level of E gene amino acid sequence difference between vaccine strains and viruses from VCD cases in CYD14 and CYD15 was <3% for all serotypes (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative measure of sequence similarity between vaccine and wild-type strains.

claim: Positions of amino acid non-identity between CYD-TDV vaccine strains and wild-type viruses were dispersed across the E protein and do not cluster to any particular structural domain.
source: These data reveal that positions of amino acid non-identity between CYD-TDV vaccine strains and wild-type viruses were dispersed across the E protein and do not cluster to any particular structural domain.
evidence: The manuscript describes the distribution pattern of amino acid differences based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Sequence analyses indicated limited variation at epitope regions targeted by neutralizing human mAbs in the CYD14/15 sequences.
source: Sequence analyses indicated limited variation at these epitope regions in the CYD14/15 sequences, as well as in a global database of wild-type virus sequences (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from sequence analysis of epitope regions.

claim: The conservation of epitope sequences between decades-old donor viruses and contemporary virus populations suggests that these amino acid sites are not highly prone to evolutionary drift.
source: The conservation of these epitope sequences between the decades-old 'donor' viruses from which the CYD-TDV product was derived and contemporary virus populations suggests that these amino acid sites are not highly prone to evolutionary drift.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the observed sequence conservation.

claim: For DENV-1, vaccine efficacy estimates against the three different genotypes were highly similar in the all ages group.
source: For DENV-1, vaccine efficacy estimates against the three different genotypes were highly similar in the all ages group and in participants 9–16 years of age (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports vaccine efficacy results for DENV-1 genotypes.

claim: For DENV-1, the genotype interaction parameter estimates in the all ages group were close to zero and had reasonably tight 95% confidence bounds.
source: Additionally, the genotype interaction parameter estimates in the all ages group (Table 3) were close to zero and had reasonably tight 95% confidence bounds.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results for DENV-1.

claim: For DENV-2, vaccine efficacy against the American-Asian genotype was 50.2% (95% CI: 32.6–63.2%) in the all ages group.
source: For DENV-2, vaccine efficacy estimates against the American-Asian genotype (50.2%; 95% CI: 32.6–63.2%) and the Cosmopolitan genotype (43.8%; 95% CI: 16.1–62.2%) were similar, and both were higher than against the Asian I genotype (19.8%; 95% CI: −30.0–49.6%) in the all ages group (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific vaccine efficacy estimates with confidence intervals.

claim: For DENV-2, vaccine efficacy against the Cosmopolitan genotype was 43.8% (95% CI: 16.1–62.2%) in the all ages group.
source: For DENV-2, vaccine efficacy estimates against the American-Asian genotype (50.2%; 95% CI: 32.6–63.2%) and the Cosmopolitan genotype (43.8%; 95% CI: 16.1–62.2%) were similar, and both were higher than against the Asian I genotype (19.8%; 95% CI: −30.0–49.6%) in the all ages group (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific vaccine efficacy estimates with confidence intervals.

claim: For DENV-2, vaccine efficacy against the Asian I genotype was 19.8% (95% CI: −30.0–49.6%) in the all ages group.
source: For DENV-2, vaccine efficacy estimates against the American-Asian genotype (50.2%; 95% CI: 32.6–63.2%) and the Cosmopolitan genotype (43.8%; 95% CI: 16.1–62.2%) were similar, and both were higher than against the Asian I genotype (19.8%; 95% CI: −30.0–49.6%) in the all ages group (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific vaccine efficacy estimates with confidence intervals.

claim: Against DENV-4, vaccine efficacy was significantly lower against genotype I (58.3%, 95% CI: 29.9–75.2%) compared to genotype II (81.8%, 95% CI: 74.3–87.1%) in the all ages population (p=0.009).
source: Against DENV-4, vaccine efficacy was significantly lower against genotype I (58.3%, 95% CI: 29.9–75.2%), which circulates endemically only in Asia, compared to the globally distributed genotype II (81.8%, 95% CI: 74.3–87.1%, across CYD14/CYD15) in the all ages population (p=0.009) (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific vaccine efficacy estimates with confidence intervals and statistical significance.

claim: DENV-4 genotype I circulates endemically only in Asia.
source: Against DENV-4, vaccine efficacy was significantly lower against genotype I (58.3%, 95% CI: 29.9–75.2%), which circulates endemically only in Asia, compared to the globally distributed genotype II (81.8%, 95% CI: 74.3–87.1%, across CYD14/CYD15) in the all ages population (p=0.009) (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the geographic distribution of DENV-4 genotype I.

claim: DENV-4 genotype II is globally distributed.
source: Against DENV-4, vaccine efficacy was significantly lower against genotype I (58.3%, 95% CI: 29.9–75.2%), which circulates endemically only in Asia, compared to the globally distributed genotype II (81.8%, 95% CI: 74.3–87.1%, across CYD14/CYD15) in the all ages population (p=0.009) (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the geographic distribution of DENV-4 genotype II.

claim: When efficacy against DENV-4 genotype I versus genotype II was considered only in participants ≥ 9 years, efficacy was similar between genotypes.
source: However, when efficacy against DENV-4 genotype I versus genotype II was considered only in participants ≥ 9 years, efficacy was similar between genotypes (Table 2) and confidence intervals for interaction estimates included zero (Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports subgroup analysis results for DENV-4 in older participants.

claim: CYD-TDV was found to be safe and efficacious for use in children 9 years of age and older.
source: CYD-TDV was found to be safe and efficacious for use in children 9 years of age and older, with efficacy varying according to age, baseline serostatus and virus serotype (Capeding et al., 2014; Villar et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that established vaccine safety and efficacy.

claim: CYD-TDV efficacy varies according to age, baseline serostatus and virus serotype.
source: CYD-TDV was found to be safe and efficacious for use in children 9 years of age and older, with efficacy varying according to age, baseline serostatus and virus serotype (Capeding et al., 2014; Villar et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that documented variation in vaccine efficacy.

claim: A trend toward reduced efficacy against DENV-2 was observed in the Asian phase III trial compared to the Latin American trial.
source: Furthermore, a trend toward reduced efficacy against DENV-2 was observed in the Asian phase III trial compared to the Latin American trial (Hadinegoro et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that observed this trend.

claim: Dengue is the commonest arboviral disease of humans.
source: Dengue is the commonest arboviral disease of humans and has been a major public health problem in tropical Asia and Latin America for decades (Stanaway et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about dengue disease burden.

claim: Dengue has been a major public health problem in tropical Asia and Latin America for decades.
source: Dengue is the commonest arboviral disease of humans and has been a major public health problem in tropical Asia and Latin America for decades (Stanaway et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about dengue disease burden.

claim: Dengue viruses exist as four phylogenetically and antigenically distinct serotypes (DENV-1 to −4).
source: Dengue vaccine development has been challenging, in part because dengue viruses (DENV) exist as four phylogenetically and antigenically distinct serotypes (DENV-1 to −4).
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about DENV classification.

claim: Within each virus serotype exists considerable genetic diversity at local, national and continental scales.
source: Within each virus serotype exists considerable genetic diversity at local, national and continental scales (Holmes, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about DENV genetic diversity.

claim: Subtle antigenic differences can be measured amongst members of the same virus serotype.
source: Subtle antigenic differences can also be measured amongst members of the same virus serotype and are speculated to be of epidemiological and clinical importance (Katzelnick et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites research on antigenic variation within serotypes.

claim: Antigenic differences within serotypes are speculated to be of epidemiological and clinical importance.
source: Subtle antigenic differences can also be measured amongst members of the same virus serotype and are speculated to be of epidemiological and clinical importance (Katzelnick et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites speculation about the importance of antigenic variation.

claim: The CYD14 trial involved more than 31,000 children between the ages of 2–14 years in the Asia–Pacific region.
source: Two phase III efficacy trials of CYD-TDV, involving more than 31,000 children between the ages of 2–14 years in the Asia–Pacific region (CYD14 trial) and between the ages of 9–16 years in Latin America (CYD15 trial) (Hadinegoro et al., 2015) enable, for the first time, a post hoc investigation of vaccine efficacy versus DENV population diversity.
evidence: The manuscript cites the trial design and population.

claim: The CYD15 trial involved children between the ages of 9–16 years in Latin America.
source: Two phase III efficacy trials of CYD-TDV, involving more than 31,000 children between the ages of 2–14 years in the Asia–Pacific region (CYD14 trial) and between the ages of 9–16 years in Latin America (CYD15 trial) (Hadinegoro et al., 2015) enable, for the first time, a post hoc investigation of vaccine efficacy versus DENV population diversity.
evidence: The manuscript cites the trial design and population.

claim: The DENV E protein components in the CYD-TDV formulation shared high-level amino acid sequence identity with viruses sampled in the CYD14 and CYD15 trials.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the DENV E protein components in the CYD-TDV formulation shared high-level amino acid sequence identity, including at prominent B cell epitopes targeted by virus neutralising human mAbs, with viruses sampled in the CYD14 and CYD15 trials.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from sequence analysis.

claim: High-level amino acid sequence identity was observed at prominent B cell epitopes targeted by virus neutralising human mAbs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the DENV E protein components in the CYD-TDV formulation shared high-level amino acid sequence identity, including at prominent B cell epitopes targeted by virus neutralising human mAbs, with viruses sampled in the CYD14 and CYD15 trials.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from epitope sequence analysis.

claim: Limited statistical evidence of genotype-specific differences in the efficacy profile was found within the constraints of the available sample size.
source: Additionally, within the constraints of the available sample size and confounding factors discussed later, we found limited statistical evidence of genotype-specific differences in the efficacy profile.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from statistical analysis of vaccine efficacy.

claim: This study provides a contemporary characterization of DENV population genetics in ten highly endemic countries.
source: With a total of 253 DENV-1, 191 DENV-2, 107 DENV-3 and 110 DENV-4 E gene sequences generated from CYD14 and CYD15, this study provides a contemporary characterization of DENV population genetics in ten highly endemic countries.
evidence: The manuscript describes the scope and contribution of the sequence data.

claim: The E gene phylogenies positioned the CYD14 and CYD15 sequences together with those from geographically identical locations.
source: Across all four serotypes, the E gene phylogenies positioned the CYD14 and CYD15 sequences together with those from geographically identical locations, consistent with long-term endemic circulation of a single virus genotype within each viral serotype in nearly all locations.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The phylogeographical profile demonstrates within-region sharing of virus genotypes but little inter-regional mixing.
source: Additionally, the phylogeographical profile demonstrates within-region sharing of virus genotypes but little inter-regional mixing (distinct viral population profiles can be distinguished within three major geographical categories: mainland Southeast Asia, maritime Southeast Asia, the Americas); only DENV-4 genotype II was found in multiple countries in both regions.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from phylogeographic analysis.

claim: Only DENV-4 genotype II was found in multiple countries in both Asia and the Americas.
source: Additionally, the phylogeographical profile demonstrates within-region sharing of virus genotypes but little inter-regional mixing (distinct viral population profiles can be distinguished within three major geographical categories: mainland Southeast Asia, maritime Southeast Asia, the Americas); only DENV-4 genotype II was found in multiple countries in both regions.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from phylogeographic analysis.

claim: The number of genotypes detected for any given serotype was greater in Southeast Asia than in Latin America.
source: The number of genotypes, and hence genetic diversity, detected for any given serotype was greater in Southeast Asia than in Latin America, as expected given the long history of hyperendemicity, within-serotype diversity, and high forces of infection in Southeast Asia (Halstead, 2006; Holmes, 2009; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2014; Imai et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from genotype analysis and cites supporting literature.

claim: Indonesia had two DENV-1 genotypes in co-circulation during the trial.
source: Indonesia, with two DENV-1 genotypes, and the Philippines, with two DENV-4 genotypes, were the only countries with genotype co-circulation detected within the trial.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from genotype analysis.

claim: The Philippines had two DENV-4 genotypes in co-circulation during the trial.
source: Indonesia, with two DENV-1 genotypes, and the Philippines, with two DENV-4 genotypes, were the only countries with genotype co-circulation detected within the trial.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from genotype analysis.

claim: Indonesia and the Philippines were the only countries with genotype co-circulation detected within the trial.
source: Indonesia, with two DENV-1 genotypes, and the Philippines, with two DENV-4 genotypes, were the only countries with genotype co-circulation detected within the trial.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from genotype analysis.

claim: Immunization of non-human primates with CYD-TDV elicited antibodies that neutralised geographically, phylogenetically and clinically diverse DENV serotypes and genotypes.
source: With respect to CYD-TDV, immunization of non-human primates elicited antibodies that neutralised geographically, phylogenetically and clinically diverse DENV serotypes and genotypes (Barban et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on vaccine immunogenicity.

claim: CYD-TDV immunisation induced similar measured levels of efficacy against all genotypes of DENV-1.
source: That CYD-TDV immunisation induced similar measured levels of efficacy against all genotypes of DENV-1 is supportive of the concept that clinical immunity elicited by CYD-TDV to this serotype was pan-genotype in nature (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from vaccine efficacy analysis.

claim: In a previous phase IIb trial (CYD23) in Thai children, all circulating DENV-2 viruses belonged to the Asian I genotype.
source: In a previous, single-centre phase IIb trial (CYD23) in Thai children (Sabchareon et al., 2012), where all the circulating DENV-2 viruses belonged to the Asian I genotype, efficacy was just 3.5% (-59.8; 40.5) against this serotype/genotype.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous trial data.

claim: In the CYD23 trial, efficacy against DENV-2 Asian I genotype was 3.5% (-59.8; 40.5).
source: In a previous, single-centre phase IIb trial (CYD23) in Thai children (Sabchareon et al., 2012), where all the circulating DENV-2 viruses belonged to the Asian I genotype, efficacy was just 3.5% (-59.8; 40.5) against this serotype/genotype.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous trial data.

claim: The parental strain of the CYD DENV-2 component is based on an historical Asian I strain.
source: Interestingly, while the parental strain of the CYD DENV-2 component is in fact based on an historical Asian I strain, contemporary DENV-2 Asian I populations diverge from the parental CYD strain at multiple amino acid residues, some of which are postulated to increase transmission fitness in some circumstances (Vu et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript states the origin of the vaccine component and cites supporting literature.

claim: Contemporary DENV-2 Asian I populations diverge from the parental CYD strain at multiple amino acid residues.
source: Interestingly, while the parental strain of the CYD DENV-2 component is in fact based on an historical Asian I strain, contemporary DENV-2 Asian I populations diverge from the parental CYD strain at multiple amino acid residues, some of which are postulated to increase transmission fitness in some circumstances (Vu et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from sequence analysis and cites supporting literature.

claim: Some amino acid residues where contemporary DENV-2 Asian I diverges from the CYD strain are postulated to increase transmission fitness.
source: Interestingly, while the parental strain of the CYD DENV-2 component is in fact based on an historical Asian I strain, contemporary DENV-2 Asian I populations diverge from the parental CYD strain at multiple amino acid residues, some of which are postulated to increase transmission fitness in some circumstances (Vu et al., 2010).

claim: The licensure of CYD-TDV provided the first prospects of an integrated public health approach to dengue disease control.
source: Accordingly, the licensure of the first tetravalent dengue vaccine (chimeric yellow fever–dengue virus tetravalent dengue vaccine (CYD-TDV), Sanofi Pasteur) together with recommendations from The World Health Organisation's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on Immunization on its use in highly endemic countries, has provided the first prospects of an integrated public health approach to disease control (WHO, 2016).
